analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to disclose toxic chemical releases and chemicals in children's products, and expands the public's right to know about chemical use.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 148 cosponsors in the House but was never acted on by the Commerce Committee, dying in a subcommittee before any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded the nation's toxic release reporting system. Companies would have to report releases of lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, and chromium at much lower thresholds, disclose toxic chemicals contained in toys and other children's products, and reveal how much of each toxic chemical they bring in, use, and ship out each year. It also let citizens sue to enforce the new reporting rules and made it easier for the public to find all environmental data about a company in one place.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents, children, and people living near industrial facilities gain access to information about toxic chemicals in their neighborhoods and in products their children use. Disclosure requirements of this kind historically push companies to reduce the chemicals they release, because public reporting creates pressure to cut emissions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents, children, and communities near polluting facilities

how_it_helps.text: Lowers reporting thresholds for chemicals that build up in the body, including lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, and chromium, so that releases covering at least 80 percent of each chemical must be publicly reported, and the bill found that disclosure requirements have been shown to prompt those causing risks to reduce them [S2] [S3].

Requires manufacturers of toys and other children's products to report to the Consumer Product Safety Commission any cancer-causing, nerve-damaging, or reproductive-toxic chemicals in those products, with the information published annually and made available electronically to the public [S2] [S3].

Expands toxic release forms to include how many workers are exposed to each chemical at a facility and annual materials accounting — how much of each toxic chemical enters, is used, and leaves a facility — giving communities a fuller picture than release data alone [S2] [S3].

Authorizes citizen lawsuits against companies that fail to report and against agencies that fail to carry out their duties, with attorney fees available to prevailing citizens, and lets courts direct penalties toward public awareness projects [S2] [S3].

Requires the EPA to consolidate all annual environmental reporting for small businesses into one form and to give the public a single point of contact for all environmental information the agency holds on any regulated company [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and other industrial facilities bear the cost of measuring and reporting lower-level releases, chemicals used in-house, and materials accounting data. Toy makers and, after three years, all consumer product manufacturers must test for and report listed toxic chemicals in their products. Some of these costs could be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers, industrial facilities, and toy manufacturers

drawbacks.text: The reporting burden falls on businesses, including smaller manufacturers, and the bill itself acknowledges this by requiring the EPA to consolidate reporting into a single form for small businesses [S2] [S3].

Disclosure alone does not ban anything or set a safety limit; it creates public pressure and information but leaves decisions about whether a chemical in a toy is dangerous to existing regulators and to lawsuits, which can be slow and uneven [S2].

The bill allows companies to withhold portions of materials accounting information as trade secrets, which means the public would not always see the full picture of how chemicals move through a facility [S2] [S3].

Critics of expanded reporting have long argued that releasing production and use data publicly can expose confidential business information and impose compliance costs without directly reducing any health risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits were entirely informational: no chemical would have been banned, but communities and parents would have learned what toxic chemicals were being released nearby and put in children's products, and disclosure rules of this type have historically pushed companies to cut their use of reported chemicals. The costs were real but ordinary for environmental reporting — measurement, paperwork, and some loss of competitive privacy, softened by trade-secret exemptions and consolidated small-business reporting. The main design weakness is that it relies on public pressure rather than enforcement standards to change behavior.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with 148 cosponsors and sent to the House Commerce Committee, which referred it to a subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no floor action, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Children's Environmental Protection and Right to Know Act of 1997 on May 15, 1997, joined by an initial group of about 90 House members [S1] [S3] [S5].
The bill attracted 148 cosponsors — 133 Democrats, 14 Republicans, and 1 independent — giving it substantial bipartisan-looking support on paper [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce on May 15, 1997, and on May 29, 1997, to its Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor consideration, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and toy and consumer product makers were better off, because the expanded disclosure requirements that would have applied to them never took effect. Parents and communities near industrial facilities lost the information the bill would have made public.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited an initial roster of roughly 90 cosigning members [S3] [S5].

for.name: 148 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support: 133 Democrats, 14 Republicans, and 1 independent [S4].

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Thomas Bliley, R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 15, 1997, referred it to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials, and never reported it out; no markup or hearing appears in the record [S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 29, 1997 onward with no recorded action before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (133 of 148) with modest Republican support (14), so the bill's evident backing came mostly from one party while the committee controlling its fate was run by the other.

industries.note: The bill would have required reporting of lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, chromium, and other bioaccumulative chemicals at far lower thresholds, plus disclosure of how chemicals are used in-house — more public visibility and more pressure to reduce use. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against the public's interest in knowing about toxic releases [S2] [S3].

They would have had to report cancer-causing, neurotoxic, or reproductive-toxic chemicals contained in toys and other children's products to the Consumer Product Safety Commission, with the list published to the public; after three years the requirement would have extended to all consumer products [S2] [S3].

Facilities would have faced expanded reporting on occupational exposures, materials accounting, and additional industry categories, plus consolidated reporting requirements — new compliance costs balanced in part by a single streamlined form and a trade-secret withholding option [S2] [S3].
